Building strings
The += operator allows us to write this a little more compactly, this also applies to f-strings, which may come in handy if values stored in variables are needed as parts of the resulting string. For example this would work:
course = "Introduction to Programming"
grade = 4

text:
String
The * operator can also be used with a string, when the other operand is an integer.
The string operand is then repeated the number of times specified by the integer. For example this would work:
word = "banana"
print(word*3)
Sample output
bananabananabanana

As strings are essentially sequences of characters, any single character in a string can also be retrieved. The operator [] finds the character with the index specified within the brackets.

The index refers to a position in the string, counting up from zero. The first character in the string has index 0, the second character has index 1, and so forth.







The index refers to a position in the string


For example, this program
input_string = input("Please type in a string: ")
print(input_string[0])
print(input_string[1])
print(input_string[3])
would print out this:
Sample output
Please type in a string: monkey
m
o
k

IndexError: string index out of range
If you tried the above examples for yourself, you may already have come across the error message IndexError: string index out of range.

This error appears if you try to access an index which is not present in the string.

input_string = input("Please type in a string: ")
print("The tenth character: " + input_string[9])
Sample output
Please type in a string: introduction to programming
The tenth character: i
Sample output

File "", line 1, in

title: Python Helsinki: 3
text:
Substrings and slices

A substring of a string is a sequence of characters that forms a part of the string.
For example, the string example contains the substrings exam, amp and ple, among others.

In Python programming, the process of selecting substrings is usually called slicing, and a substring is often referred to as a slice of the string. The two terms can often be used interchangeably.
If you know the beginning and end indexes of the slice you wish to extract, you can do so with the notation [a:b]. This means the slice begins at the index a and ends at the last character before index b - that is, including the first, but excluding the last.
You can think of the indexes as separator lines drawn on the left side of the indexed character, as illustrated in the image below:







You can think of the indexes as separator lines drawn on the left side of the indexed character


Let’s have a closer look at some sliced strings:
input_string = "presumptious"

print(input_string[0:3])
print(input_string[4:10])

# if the beginning index is left out, it defaults to 0
print(input_string[:3])

# if the end index is left out, it defaults to the length of the string
print(input_string[4:])
Sample output
pre
umptio
pre
umptious






Half open intervals



In Python string processing the interval [a:b] is half open, which in this case means that the character at the beginning index a is included in the interval, but the character at the end index b is left out.
Why is that?
There is no profound reason for this feature. Rather it is a convention inherited from other programming languages.
Half open intervals may feel unintuitive, but in practice they do have some advantages. For example, you can easily calculate the length of a slice with b-a. On the other hand, you must always remember that the character at the end index b will not be included in the slice.

The Boolean expression a in b is true, if b contains the substring a.

Instead, the Python string method find can be used for this purpose.

It takes the substring searched for as an argument, and returns either the first index where it is found, or -1 if the substring is not found within the string.

title: Python Helsinki: 3
text:
Else without if
In Python, a while loop can have an else block without an if statement. This structure is unique to Python and can be useful in certain scenarios. Here’s an example:
count = 0
while count < 5:
    print(f"Count: {count}")
    count += 1
else:
    print("Loop completed successfully")

In this example, the while loop executes as long as the condition count < 5 is true.
The loop body increments the count and prints its value.
Once the condition becomes false (when count reaches 5), the else block is executed.







Note



The else block in a while loop runs if the loop completes normally, without encountering a break statement.
It’s particularly useful for scenarios where you want to perform an action after a loop finishes its normal execution, such as in search algorithms or when you need to confirm that a loop has completed without interruption

The function definition
Before a function can be used, it must be defined. Any function definition begins with the keyword def, short for define. Then comes the name of the function, followed by parentheses and a colon character. This is called the header of the function. After this, indented just like while and if blocks, comes the body of the function.
For example, the following code defines the function message:
def message():
    print("This is my very own function!")

Lab#ANN002: Tensor for back propagation
A small auto-grad engine (inspired from Karpathy's micrograd and PyTorch) using Apple's MLX and Numpy. That’s why the name: smolgrad

It will help y’all understand the core concepts behind automatic differentiation and backpropagation. I mean, AI is literally powered by these things.

what is autograd?
Auto-grad, short for automatic differentiation, is a technique used in machine learning to efficiently compute gradients of complex functions. In the context of neural networks, autograd enables the computation of gradients with respect to the model’s parameters, which is crucial for training the network using optimization algorithms like gradient descent.

It works by constructing a computational graph that represents the flow of data through the network. Each node in the graph represents a mathematical operation, and the edges represent the flow of data between these operations. By tracking the operations and their dependencies, autograd can automatically compute the gradients using the chain rule of calculus.

An algorithm used in conjuction with autograd is Backpropagation to train neural networks. It is the process of propagating the gradients backward through the computational graph, from the output layer to the input layer, in order to update the model’s parameters. This is the stuff which makes ML/DL models “learn”.

title: Lab#FU01-1: Taxi fare, pure Python
text:
📘 Lab#FU01-1: Taxi fare, pure Python
In this lab you will:

Load three taxi receipts.
Guess a price per kilometre, predict, measure the error, and nudge the guess.
Repeat the loop until the guess settles on €1.50 / km.
Plot how the loss falls.

   Code on GitHub

The story starts in The learning loop. Here you run it yourself, in the page. The editor below is live Python in the browser — no install, no libraries for the loop, matplotlib only draws the loss curve. The first load takes a few seconds.
Price = w · kilometres. The true rate on these receipts is €1.50 per kilometre. You do not tell the program that number. It has to find it.

1 Creating the algorithm
The question. A taxi charges by distance. We have three receipts: 2 km cost €3, 5 km cost €7.50 and 10 km cost €15. What does 7 km cost? We don’t know the rate per kilometre, so we let the receipts teach it to us.
# TODO: find the price of a 7 km trip from three receipts
What we know and what we don’t. We know the kilometres (the input) and the prices (the answers). We don’t know the rate, which we call w. Our whole model is one line, price = w · km, and the machine’s only job is to find a good w.
km    = [2, 5, 10]       # what we know: inputs
price = [3, 7.5, 15]     # what we know: answers
# TODO: w is unknown, the thing to learn
A first guess. We have no idea, so we start badly on purpose and watch it improve.
w = 0.0                  # a bad guess on purpose
Predict. With our guess, what would each trip cost? With w = 0, every trip comes out free.
pred = [w * x for x in km]          # [0, 0, 0]
How wrong are we? We compare each prediction with the real receipt. We square the gaps, so a miss above or below counts the same and big misses count more, then average them. That number is the loss, and we want it small.
loss = sum((p - y)**2 for p, y in zip(pred, price)) / len(km)
Which way to move? Every prediction was too low, so w must go up. The gradient tells us which way and how strongly, like feeling the slope of the hill under your feet.
grad = sum(2 * (p - y) * x for p, y, x in zip(pred, price, km)) / len(km)
A small step. We nudge w a little that way. The learning rate is the step size: too small and we crawl, too big and we bounce past the bottom.
lr = 0.01
w = w - lr * grad
Again and again. We predict, measure and nudge, over and over. The loss drops and w creeps towards 1.50.
for step in range(20):
    # predict, measure, find the direction, step
    ...
When to stop. We stop when the loss barely changes, or after a fixed number of steps.
# TODO: stop when loss < 0.0001, or after N steps
Check the answer. w ≈ 1.50, so 7 km costs about €10.50. Nobody told the program the rate; it found the rate from examples. That’s learning.
print(w * 7)             # ≈ 10.5


2 Guess, predict, error, nudge
Three rides: 2 km for €3, 5 km for €7.50, 10 km for €15. Start at \(w = 0\) — every ride is free — and take steps of size \(0.01\).
The gradient of the mean squared error is the average of \(2 \cdot \text{error} \cdot \text{km}\). A nudge is a small step against that gradient:
\[
w \leftarrow w - 0.01 \cdot \nabla L
\]






Try it



Change learning_rate and press Run. Try a smaller rate, or a larger one.








After the first nudge, \(w\) jumps from \(0\) to \(1.29\). After four steps it is already \(1.4994\). By step 6 it has settled on \(1.50\). Nobody programmed the rate.
Loss starts at \(96.75\) — every ride predicted as free — and drops to about zero once \(w\) reaches \(1.50\).






Reading the code: mean_squared_error





This little function answers one question: how wrong is this weight? Let’s run it by hand with weight = 1.

predictions: what we would charge with this weight: 2, 5, 10.
errors: prediction minus real price: −1, −2.5, −5. Negative means we charged too little.
e * e: square each error: 1, 6.25, 25.
sum(...) / len(km): add them (32.25) and divide by the number of rides (3). The loss is 10.75.

Why square? A miss of −5 and a miss of +5 are equally bad, so the sign must go. And squaring makes big misses hurt much more than small ones: missing by 5 costs 25, missing by 1 costs only 1.
In maths it is written:
\[
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (w \cdot x_i - y_i)^2
\]
Same thing as the code: for every ride, predict, subtract the real price, square, then take the average. With weight = 0 you get the 96.75 above; with weight = 1.5 you get 0. See the MSE card, \(\Sigma\) summation and The loss is a landscape.

title: Optimization essentials
text:
The loss is a landscape
Training asks: which parameters make the error smaller? Write that error as a loss \(L(\theta)\). If you imagine \(L\) as height, the parameters sit on a landscape. A good model is a low point.
The formal question is \(\arg\min_\theta L(\theta)\): which \(\theta\) gives the smallest loss? See \(\arg\min\) on the symbols page. We rarely solve that in one shot. We walk downhill instead.








A loss bowl with gradient-descent steps walking from a starting point to the minimum.











A loss bowl with gradient-descent steps walking from a starting point to the minimum.





The gradient descent update
The gradient \(\nabla L\) (see calculus and the \(\nabla\) card) points uphill. A step the other way is
\[
\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\nabla L(\theta),
\]
where \(\eta>0\) is the learning rate. A one-weight program that repeats this step is on The learning loop.
A tiny numeric example. Let \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\), so \(\nabla L=2(w-3)\). Start at \(w=5\) with \(\eta=0.1\) (the same toy loss as on the calculus page):
\[
w \leftarrow 5 - 0.1\times 4 = 4.6.
\]
The loss falls from \(4\) to \(2.56\). Repeat, and \(w\) drifts toward \(3\), where the slope is zero.


The learning rate: too small or too big








Three walks on the same bowl: a tiny learning rate crawls, a good one settles, a large one diverges.











Three walks on the same bowl: a tiny learning rate crawls, a good one settles, a large one diverges.



If \(\eta\) is too small, each step is a shuffle and training crawls. If \(\eta\) is too big, the step overshoots the valley and the loss can bounce or blow up. A good rate is large enough to make progress and small enough to settle.


Batch, stochastic, and mini-batch
The gradient is an average over examples.

Batch (full-batch) uses every example at once. The path is smooth, but one step can be slow when the dataset is large.
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) uses one example (or one very small draw). The path is noisy, which is cheaper per step and can help the walk leave a shallow dip.
Mini-batch takes a small group, often tens or hundreds of rows. This is the usual compromise: a stabler gradient than one row, still cheap enough to run on a GPU.



Momentum
Plain steps can zigzag down a long, narrow valley: each step dives toward a wall, then back. Momentum keeps a running average of recent gradients and steps in that direction, so the walk builds speed along the valley and damps the zigzag.








Two paths on a narrow valley: plain gradient descent zigzags, momentum makes steadier progress.











Two paths on a narrow valley: plain gradient descent zigzags, momentum makes steadier progress.





Adam, in one idea
Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) is a very common default. The name is short for adaptive moment estimation. It keeps two running averages: one of the gradient (a momentum term) and one of the squared gradient (how large that parameter’s slopes have been). Parameters that have been seeing large, noisy slopes get a smaller effective step; quieter ones get a larger one. You still choose a base learning rate, but each parameter then adapts its own pace.


Local minima and saddle points
A local minimum is a dip that is lower than its neighbours, but not necessarily the lowest point on the whole landscape (the global minimum). A saddle point is a pass: uphill in some directions, downhill in others. In a high-dimensional loss, the walk can slow down near saddles, where the slope is almost flat. Mini-batch noise and methods such as momentum often help the walk keep moving.


A tiny NumPy walk
import numpy as np

# L(w) = (w - 3)**2, start at 5, learning rate 0.1
w, eta = 5.0, 0.1
for _ in range(5):
    grad = 2 * (w - 3)
    w = w - eta * grad
    print(w, (w - 3)**2)
# 4.6      2.56
# 4.28     1.6384
# 4.024    1.048576
# 3.8192   0.67108864
# 3.65536  0.4294967296
The slopes that feed this update come from the chain rule and, in a network, from the activation functions along the way.

title: Calculus essentials
text:
A derivative is a slope
If \(y=f(x)\), the derivative \(f'(x)\) (also written \(\frac{dy}{dx}\)) is the slope of \(f\) at \(x\): how fast \(y\) rises or falls if \(x\) moves a little.
A straight line \(y=3x+1\) has slope \(3\) everywhere. A curve \(y=x^2\) has slope \(2x\): at \(x=2\) the slope is \(4\), at \(x=0\) it is flat.
For a picture of a steep slope versus a gentle one, see the gradient primer on the activation-functions page.


Partial derivatives and the gradient \(\nabla\)
When a function has several inputs, a partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x\) asks: how fast does \(f\) change if I move only \(x\), and hold the other inputs still?
The gradient \(\nabla f\) is the vector of all those partials. It points in the direction of steepest increase. To reduce a loss, we step the other way.
A tiny example. \(f(x,y)=x^2+3y\) at \((2,1)\): \(\partial f/\partial x=4\), \(\partial f/\partial y=3\), so \(\nabla f=(4,3)\).


The chain rule, which backpropagation rests on
If a value is a function of a function, \(y=f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\), the slopes multiply:
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=f'\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\cdot g'(x).
\]
A tiny example. \(y=(2x+1)^2\). Let \(u=2x+1\). Then \(\frac{dy}{dx}=2u\cdot 2=4(2x+1)\). At \(x=1\), the slope is \(12\).
A neural network is a long chain: input, then \(xW+b\), then an activation, then the next layer, then a loss. Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to that chain, from the loss back to each weight. If an activation has a tiny slope, the product shrinks; that is the vanishing-gradient story on the activation-functions page.
# y = (2x + 1)**2 at x = 1, numerical check of the slope 12
h = 1e-6
x = 1.0
(((2*(x+h)+1)**2) - ((2*(x-h)+1)**2)) / (2*h)   # about 12


Gradient descent, one step
To reduce a loss \(L(w)\), move against the gradient:
\[
w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\nabla L(w),
\]
where \(\eta\) (the learning rate) is a small positive step size.
A tiny numeric example. Let \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\), so \(\nabla L=2(w-3)\). Start at \(w=5\) with \(\eta=0.1\):
\[
w \leftarrow 5 - 0.1\times 4 = 4.6.
\]
The loss goes from \((5-3)^2=4\) to \((4.6-3)^2=2.56\). One more step: \(4.6-0.1\times 3.2=4.28\), and the loss falls again. Repeat until the slope is almost zero (here, at \(w=3\)).
w, lr = 5.0, 0.1
for _ in range(3):
    grad = 2 * (w - 3)
    w = w - lr * grad
    print(w, (w - 3)**2)
# 4.6  2.56
# 4.28 1.6384
# 4.024 1.0486...





flowchart TD
  A[Compute the loss] --> B[Compute the gradient]
  B --> C["Step: w = w minus lr times grad"]
  C --> A

title: ML math symbols, explained easy
text:
The core symbols
A short deck of the symbols you will keep seeing. Each card has one question, a figure, an everyday example, a tiny numerical example, and a NumPy line.


\(\nabla\) — gradient
In one line. Which direction should the parameters move to reduce the loss?








Gradient = which way is downhill.











Gradient = which way is downhill.









Everyday example



You are on the top of a hill, and the next step will make you go down. What is the gradient of this step, the direction of this step? This movement is very important. It’s easy.


Analogy. You are standing on a hill in the fog. The gradient points uphill. To reduce the loss, take a step the other way.
A tiny example. Let \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\). At \(w=5\), the slope is \(2(w-3)=4\). A descent step moves left: \(w\leftarrow 5-0.1\times 4=4.6\), closer to \(3\).
w, lr, grad = 5.0, 0.1, 4.0
w = w - lr * grad   # 4.6
Where it shows up. Gradient descent, and every backward pass. The learning loop is that nudge, repeated. See Calculus essentials and the gradient primer.


\(\mathbb{E}\) — expectation
In one line. What is the average value over all possible outcomes, weighted by probability?








Expectation = a weighted average.











Expectation = a weighted average.









Everyday example



If you take the same bus every morning, some days it is early and some days it is late. The expectation is the average time you would see if you did this for many mornings — not any single day. A loss in a model is the same idea: the average error over many examples.


Analogy. The long-run average if you repeated the same random experiment many times. A fair die has expectation \(3.5\), even though \(3.5\) never appears on a face.
A tiny example. Outcomes \(2\), \(4\), \(10\) with probabilities \(0.5\), \(0.25\), \(0.25\): \(\mathbb{E}[x]=2\cdot 0.5+4\cdot 0.25+10\cdot 0.25=4.5\).
import numpy as np
x, p = np.array([2.0, 4.0, 10.0]), np.array([0.5, 0.25, 0.25])
np.dot(x, p)   # 4.5
Where it shows up. A loss is often an expectation — the average error over data. See Probability and statistics.


\(\odot\) — element-wise multiplication
In one line. Multiply corresponding entries, not entire matrices.








⊙ multiplies matching cells; a matrix product mixes rows and columns.











⊙ multiplies matching cells; a matrix product mixes rows and columns.









Everyday example



You have a shopping list and a “how many I already have” list, item by item: apples with apples, milk with milk. You never mix the apple line with the milk line. In a network, a gate does the same: it keeps or kills each number in its own place.


Analogy. Two shopping lists, item by item. You never mix the apple row with the orange row — that mix would be a matrix product.
A tiny example. \((1,2,3)\odot(4,5,6)=(4,10,18)\).
import numpy as np
np.array([1, 2, 3]) * np.array([4, 5, 6])   # [4, 10, 18]
Where it shows up. LSTM gates (forget gate \(\odot\) cell state), attention masks, and any “keep or kill this entry” operation. See Linear algebra essentials.


\(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) — norm
In one line. How big is a vector or an error?








A vector with its L2 length and the L1 taxi path.











A vector with its L2 length and the L1 taxi path.









Everyday example



To the shop, you can cut across the park (the straight path) or walk the street corners like a taxi. Both answer “how far is it?” — one as a straight line, one as the blocks you actually walk. In ML, a norm asks how big a vector or an error is.


Analogy. The length of an arrow. The everyday L2 (Euclidean) norm is the straight-line distance, the same rule as Pythagoras. The L1 norm is the taxi-city walk, along the axes.
A tiny example. For \(v=(3,4)\), \(\lVert v\rVert_2=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\) and \(\lVert v\rVert_1=3+4=7\). A loss often uses the squared L2 norm, \(25\), so the square root can be skipped.
import numpy as np
np.linalg.norm([3.0, 4.0])   # 5.0
Where it shows up. Distance to a cluster centre (k-means inertia), L2 regularisation \(\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2\), and “how large is this error?”. See k-means and Linear algebra essentials.


\(\arg\max\) — argmax
In one line. Which input gives the highest value?








A curve with the peak marked; argmax is the x-position, max is the height.











A curve with the peak marked; argmax is the x-position, max is the height.









Everyday example



The league table shows the scores, but what you care about is which team finished first, not only how many points they got. That “which one?” is argmax. A classifier does the same: it picks the class with the highest score.


Analogy. Not “how high did the class score?”, but “which class won?”.
A tiny example. Scores \((0.1, 0.7, 0.2)\): the maximum is \(0.7\), and \(\arg\max\) is index \(1\) (the second class, counting from \(0\)).
import numpy as np
np.argmax([0.1, 0.7, 0.2])   # 1
Where it shows up. The predicted class in a classifier: take the output scores (or a softmax) and return \(\arg\max\).


A few more that complete the set


\(\Sigma\) — summation
In one line. Add these terms up.








Bars of 1, 2 and 3 stacking into a total of 6.











Bars of 1, 2 and 3 stacking into a total of 6.









Everyday example



At the till, you add every line on the receipt to get the total. Sigma is just that: plus, plus, plus, written small. Almost every loss adds up the errors in the same way.


Analogy. A running total. The sigma sign is a compact “plus, plus, plus”.
A tiny example. \(\sum_{i=1}^{3} i = 1+2+3=6\). A mean is just a sum divided by the count: \((1+2+3)/3=2\).
import numpy as np
np.sum([1, 2, 3])   # 6
Where it shows up. Almost every loss and every mean: inertia, cross-entropy, sum of squared errors.


\(\prod\) — product
In one line. Multiply these terms together.








0.9 times 0.5 times 0.2 equals 0.09.











0.9 times 0.5 times 0.2 equals 0.09.









Everyday example



Three locks on a bike: the bike is free only if lock 1 and lock 2 and lock 3 are open. When the steps are independent, you multiply the chances. That is how a naïve likelihood treats independent clues.


Analogy. A chain of “and”s: the chance that several independent things all happen is the product of their chances.
A tiny example. \(0.9\times 0.5\times 0.2=0.09\).
import numpy as np
np.prod([0.9, 0.5, 0.2])   # 0.09
Where it shows up. The likelihood of independent events, and the “naïve” product inside Naïve Bayes. Long products of probabilities get tiny, which is why we usually take a \(\log\) next.


\(\log\) — logarithm
In one line. Turn a product into a sum, and stretch small probabilities so they are easier to add and to compare.








A product 0.5 × 0.4 becoming log 0.5 + log 0.4, next to the log curve.











A product 0.5 × 0.4 becoming log 0.5 + log 0.4, next to the log curve.









Everyday example



A few small chances in a row — you catch the bus, the shop is open, they still have milk — make a tiny number when you multiply them, hard to read at a glance. A log turns those “times” into “plus”, so you can add them up calmly. That is why training often uses a log-likelihood or a cross-entropy.


Analogy. A translator: “times” becomes “plus”. That is why we talk about log-likelihood instead of multiplying many tiny numbers (which would underflow).
A tiny example. \(\log(0.5\times 0.4)=\log 0.5+\log 0.4=\log 0.20\). NumPy’s np.log is the natural log.
import numpy as np
np.log(0.5) + np.log(0.4)   # same as np.log(0.5 * 0.4)
Where it shows up. Log-likelihood, cross-entropy \(-\log p\), and log-softmax. See Probability and statistics.


\(\partial\) — partial derivative
In one line. How fast does this function change if I move only this input and hold the others still?








A contour with one axis held fixed, and the slope of that slice.











A contour with one axis held fixed, and the slope of that slice.









Everyday example



On a shower, you can turn only the temperature and leave the flow alone. The partial derivative asks: if I move just this knob, how fast does the water change? In a network, each weight is one knob; the gradient is the list of all those answers.


Analogy. A kitchen with two knobs, heat and time. The partial with respect to heat asks: if I turn only the heat, how fast does the cake change?
A tiny example. \(f(x,y)=x^2+3y\). At \((2,1)\), \(\partial f/\partial x=2x=4\) and \(\partial f/\partial y=3\). The gradient is the vector of both: \(\nabla f=(4,3)\).
h = 1e-6
((2+h)**2 + 3*1 - (2**2 + 3*1)) / h   # about 4
Where it shows up. A network has many parameters. The gradient \(\nabla\) is just the list of all these partials. See Calculus essentials.


\(\sigma\) — a letter with two common lives
In one line. Look at the context: \(\sigma\) may be the sigmoid function, or the standard deviation.








Two panels: a sigmoid curve, and a bell curve with the spread marked.











Two panels: a sigmoid curve, and a bell curve with the spread marked.









Everyday example



The same letter has two everyday jobs, so look at the room you are in. As a dimmer, it squashes a signal to something between off and on — that is the sigmoid in a network. As a spread, it is how much your commute time jumps around from day to day — that is the standard deviation.


Analogy. The same nickname for two classmates. In a network diagram, \(\sigma\) usually means “squash this number into \((0,1)\)”. In a statistics paragraph, \(\sigma\) is “how spread out is this data?”.
A tiny example. The sigmoid at \(0\) is \(\sigma(0)=1/(1+e^{0})=0.5\). The standard deviation of \([2,4]\) (population) is \(1\), because the mean is \(3\) and each value sits \(1\) away.
import numpy as np
1 / (1 + np.exp(0))      # sigmoid(0) = 0.5
np.std([2.0, 4.0])       # 1.0  (NumPy's default is the population std)
Where it shows up. Sigmoid activations and LSTM gates (see Activation functions); standard deviation in data summaries and in the normal distribution (see Probability and statistics).


\(^\top\) and the dot product
In one line. \(^\top\) flips rows and columns; the dot product \(u^\top v\) (or \(u\cdot v\)) multiplies matching entries and adds them up.








A 2×2 matrix flipped to its transpose, and two arrows with a projection.











A 2×2 matrix flipped to its transpose, and two arrows with a projection.









Everyday example



Turning a table on its side is a transpose: rows become columns, like flipping a seating plan. The dot product is a shopping moment: price times quantity for each item, then add — your total, and also the weighted sum inside a neuron.


Analogy. Transpose is turning a table on its corner. The dot product is “how much do these two arrows point the same way?” — or, in a neuron, a weighted sum of inputs.
A tiny example. \((1,2)\cdot(3,4)=1\cdot 3+2\cdot 4=11\). The transpose of \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\).
import numpy as np
np.dot([1, 2], [3, 4])          # 11
np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).T    # [[1, 3], [2, 4]]
Where it shows up. Almost every layer: \(x^\top w\), or a batch written as \(Xw\). See Linear algebra essentials.


\(\in\) — belongs to
In one line. Does this object belong to that set?








A point inside a set S, and a point outside.











A point inside a set S, and a point outside.









Everyday example



Is this key on your keyring, or not? Belongs-to is a simple membership check. In ML it is the same idea: this label belongs to the set of classes, this vector belongs to the space of inputs.


Analogy. A membership badge. \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) means “\(x\) is a real vector with \(n\) entries”.
A tiny example. \(3\in\{1,2,3\}\), but \(4\notin\{1,2,3\}\). A paper will write a weight matrix as \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\).
3 in {1, 2, 3}   # True
Where it shows up. Shapes and spaces: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), a label \(y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\).


\(\approx\) and \(\propto\) — approximately, proportional to
In one line. \(\approx\) means “almost equal”; \(\propto\) means “moves in proportion to” (the same shape, maybe a different scale).








A curve hugging an approximation, and two lines that scale together.











A curve hugging an approximation, and two lines that scale together.









Everyday example



The recipe says “about 180 degrees” — that is approximately, close enough. If you double the guests, you double the flour — that is proportional, the same shape at a new scale. Models use both: a handy approximation, or a posterior that follows likelihood times prior.


Analogy. \(\approx\) is a close hug, not a perfect match. \(\propto\) is “when this doubles, that doubles” — a constant factor may still be hiding.
A tiny example. \(\pi\approx 3.14\). In Bayes, the posterior is \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior (the missing piece is the normaliser \(P(\text{data})\)).
import numpy as np
np.isclose(22 / 7, 3.14, atol=0.02)   # True, roughly
# unnormalised posterior:
# posterior_unnorm = likelihood * prior
Where it shows up. Approximations such as \(\operatorname{GELU}(x)\approx x\cdot\sigma(1.702x)\), and Bayes in Probability and statistics.


\(P(A\mid B)\) — conditional probability
In one line. What is the chance of \(A\), given that we already know \(B\)?








Of the emails that contain “prize”, a slice are spam: 16/24.











Of the emails that contain “prize”, a slice are spam: 16/24.









Everyday example



You already know it is raining. Now, what is the chance you will want a coat? That is “given B, what about A?” — you have narrowed the question to the rainy days. A spam filter does the same: given this word, how likely is spam?


Analogy. Of all the emails that contain “prize”, what fraction are spam? You have already narrowed the pile to \(B\).
A tiny example. \(100\) emails, \(20\) of them spam. The word “prize” appears in \(16\) of the spam emails and in \(8\) of the rest, so in \(24\) emails altogether: \(P(\text{spam}\mid\text{prize})=16/24=2/3\).
16 / 24   # 2/3
Where it shows up. Conditioning, Bayes, and Naïve Bayes. The same example is worked on the probability page.


\(\arg\min\) and \(\min\) — the training question
In one line. \(\min\) is the smallest value; \(\arg\min\) is which input gives that smallest value. Training is \(\arg\min\) of the loss.








A loss bowl with the bottom marked: min is 0, argmin is w = 3.











A loss bowl with the bottom marked: min is 0, argmin is w = 3.









Everyday example



You are buying a phone. The lowest price is the min; which phone has that price is the argmin. Training is the same question: which parameters make the error as small as it can be?


Analogy. The lowest point on the hill (\(\min\)) versus “where do I stand to be at the bottom?” (\(\arg\min\)). The twin of \(\arg\max\).
A tiny example. For \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\), the minimum value is \(0\) and \(\arg\min_w L(w)=3\). Training writes \(\theta^\star=\arg\min_\theta L(\theta)\).
import numpy as np
ws = np.linspace(0, 6, 7)
ws[np.argmin((ws - 3)**2)]   # 3.0
Where it shows up. Every training loop: find the parameters that minimise the loss. Prediction often uses \(\arg\max\); learning uses \(\arg\min\).


MSE — mean squared error
In one line. How wrong are we, on average? Square every error, then take the mean.
\[
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2
\]
Read it right to left: for each example \(i\), take the prediction \(\hat{y}_i\) minus the real answer \(y_i\), square it, add them all up (\(\Sigma\)) and divide by how many there are (\(\frac{1}{n}\)).








Taxi receipts with w = 1: squared errors 1, 6.25 and 25 average to 10.75.











Taxi receipts with w = 1: squared errors 1, 6.25 and 25 average to 10.75.









Everyday example



You play darts and throw three. Measure how far each dart lands from the bullseye, square each distance, and average. One wild throw far from the centre ruins your score much more than three throws that are a bit off. That number is your MSE: lower is better, and 0 means every dart hit the bullseye.


Analogy. A penalty score. Small misses cost a little, big misses cost a lot, and above or below costs the same.
A tiny example. Taxi receipts 2 km for €3, 5 km for €7.50 and 10 km for €15, with a guess \(w=1\): predictions 2, 5, 10; errors −1, −2.5, −5; squared 1, 6.25, 25; mean \(32.25/3 = 10.75\). With \(w=1.5\) every error is 0, so MSE \(=0\).
km    = [2, 5, 10]
price = [3, 7.5, 15]
w = 1
errors = [w * x - y for x, y in zip(km, price)]
sum(e * e for e in errors) / len(km)   # 10.75
Where it shows up. The loss of linear regression and most regression models; the number gradient descent pushes down in Taxi Lab 1.

Generative AI Models

Generative AI models are machine learning models that can generate new data from existing data.

Generative AI models are used in many applications, such as image generation, text generation, speech synthesis, and music generation.
Table with key technologies and models that play crucial roles in Generative AI:











Technology

Comparison of three categories of generative models.




Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)

Variational AutoEncoders (VAEs) is a type of autoencoder that extends the basic architecture to learn a probabilistic model of the data.

This allows them to generate new data similar to the original input but not identical.
The key innovation in VAEs is the introduction of a regularization term known as the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, which encourages the learned distribution to match a prior distribution, typically a standard normal distribution.
This regularization term allows VAEs to generate more diverse and realistic data than traditional autoencoders.



Illustration of variational autoencoder model



From Autoencoder to Beta-VAE



Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) were introduced by Ian Goodfellow in 2014. They are a class of generative models that use two neural networks, a generator, and a discriminator, to generate new data.

The generator network takes a random noise vector as input and generates a sample from the data distribution. The discriminator network takes a sample from the data distribution and a sample from the generator network and tries to distinguish between them.

The generator network is trained to fool the discriminator network, while the discriminator network is trained to distinguish between real and fake samples.



Illustration of GAN model



From GAN to WGAN



Transformers
The Transformer was introduced in 2017 by Vaswani et al.

It is a neural network architecture that uses attention mechanisms to process data sequences.

The Transformer has been used in many applications, such as machine translation, text summarization, and image captioning.



Transformer model architecture



The Transformer Blueprint: A Holistic Guide to the Transformer Neural Network Architecture



Large Language Models (LLM)

LLMs are trained on vast amounts of textual data and use transformer models to analyze and produce coherent, contextually relevant language.

They excel at tasks such as text generation, translation, and answering questions based on their training data.

title: Deep Learning
text:
Deep learning is a transformative subset of machine learning that utilizes artificial neural networks (ANNs) to model complex patterns in data, inspired by the human brain’s architecture.
Characterized by its ability to process vast amounts of information through multiple interconnected layers, deep learning has driven significant advancements in various fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and automation.[1][2]






In this section



Start with the ANN overview and the chapter on activation functions (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh and GELU). Those pages sit just before this introduction in the Deep Learning sidebar.




The rise of deep learning has enabled machines to achieve performance levels that surpass human capabilities in tasks such as image recognition and language translation, marking a pivotal shift in how artificial intelligence (AI) is applied across industries.[1]
Notably, deep learning models, particularly deep neural networks (DNNs), have demonstrated remarkable success in diverse applications, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image analysis and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for sequential data tasks.[3][4]
However, the technology is not without its challenges; issues related to data quality, the demand for skilled professionals, and the interpretability of complex models pose significant hurdles for practitioners and organizations aiming to leverage deep learning effectively.[5][6]
Moreover, ethical concerns regarding bias and transparency in AI decision-making processes have sparked ongoing debates about the responsible development and deployment of deep learning technologies.[7][8]







AI fields


As industries increasingly rely on deep learning to enhance efficiency and innovation, understanding its foundational principles, capabilities, and limitations has become essential. The architecture of deep learning models involves intricate design choices, including layer composition and training algorithms like backpropagation, which are crucial for optimizing performance.[2][9]

With continuous research and development, the field of deep learning is poised for further growth, presenting both opportunities and challenges that must be addressed to harness its full potential in a responsible manner.



Deep learning encompasses various types of models designed to address different types of data and tasks. Each model type has its unique architecture and application area, making them suitable for specific use cases.







A comparative view of AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI (source [16]).



A comparative view of AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI (source [16]).

Deep Neural Networks and Generative AI
Deep neural networks (DNNs) extend traditional neural networks by adding multiple hidden layers, which allows them to learn more complex patterns within the data. As of 2017, DNNs typically contained thousands to millions of units and connections, enabling them to perform tasks such as image recognition and natural language processing at levels that can surpass human capabilities[1]
Each layer in a DNN builds on the previous one, allowing the model to capture intricate patterns through its architecture, which can involve convolutional layers for spatial data processing, pooling layers for dimensionality reduction, and fully connected layers for final classification tasks[9][2]

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs): Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) consist of two neural networks: a generator and a discriminator, which are trained simultaneously in a competitive framework.

The generator aims to create realistic synthetic data, while the discriminator evaluates the authenticity of the generated data against real data samples.
This adversarial training process helps improve the quality of generated outputs, making GANs popular in applications such as image generation, video creation, and data augmentation. Their ability to produce high-quality visuals has significantly impacted fields like art, entertainment, and gaming[11][12].

Transformer Models: Transformer models have gained prominence in natural language processing tasks due to their efficiency in handling sequential data without relying on recurrence.

Transformers utilize self-attention mechanisms to weigh the influence of different words in a sentence, allowing for a better understanding of context and relationships within the text.
This architecture has led to significant advancements in machine translation, text summarization, and conversational AI applications, making Transformers a crucial development in the deep learning landscape[3].

title: ANN: Activation functions
text:
What an activation function is
An activation function is a simple rule that sits at the end of a neuron: after the neuron has formed a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, the activation decides what number is sent on to the next layer.
Without it, a neuron would only ever pass along a straight-line combination of its inputs. With it, the neuron can turn off, saturate, or bend — and that is what lets a network learn curves, not just lines.





flowchart TD
  A[Inputs] --> B[Weighted sum plus bias]
  B --> C[Activation]
  C --> D[Next layer]








Why the network needs non-linearity
If every layer used only a linear map, stacking ten layers would still be one linear map. A composition of straight lines is another straight line, so the whole network could be replaced by a single layer.
A non-linear activation breaks that collapse. Each layer can now fold the space a little, and depth starts to matter. That is why ReLU, sigmoid, tanh and GELU are not decorations: they are what make a deep network actually deep.


The four, in brief
Four functions cover most of what you will meet in class and in modern models. A one-line formula and a one-line intuition for each; the details come after a short word on gradients.








Function
Formula
Intuition




ReLU
\(\max(0,x)\)
Keep the positive part; silence the rest.


Sigmoid
\(1/(1+e^{-x})\)
Squash every input into \((0,1)\).


Tanh
\(\tanh(x)\)
Squash into \((-1,1)\), centred on zero.


GELU
\(x\cdot\Phi(x)\)
A smooth ReLU that lets a little of the negative side through.











The four activations on the left, and their derivatives on the right.











The four activations on the left, and their derivatives on the right.





A gradient primer
Training moves the weights by following a gradient: the slope of the loss with respect to each weight. A handy picture is a ball on a hill. Where the hillside is steep, the slope is large and the ball rolls fast. Where the hillside is almost flat, the slope is small and the ball barely moves. For the symbol \(\nabla\) itself, and a one-step numeric descent, see ML math symbols and Calculus essentials.








A hill with a steep tangent on one side and a gentle tangent on the other. The gradient is that slope.











A hill with a steep tangent on one side and a gentle tangent on the other. The gradient is that slope.



Two practical words will keep coming back:

Cheap. Some activations are a comparison and a max (ReLU). Others need an exponential or a Gaussian CDF (sigmoid, tanh, GELU). In a big network that function is called billions of times, so a cheap slope matters.
Does not shrink. During backpropagation the incoming gradient is multiplied by the slope of the activation. If that slope is \(1\), the signal keeps its size. If the slope is \(0.2\) or \(0.01\), the signal shrinks at every layer and can vanish. If the slope is \(0\), that neuron contributes nothing to the update.



A. ReLU
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x).
\]
A negative input becomes \(0\). A positive input passes through unchanged. The gradient is \(0\) for \(x<0\) and \(1\) for \(x>0\) (the kink at \(0\) is usually given gradient \(0\)).
That is why ReLU is cheap and, for positive inputs, does not shrink the gradient. It is the default hidden activation in convolutional networks and ordinary MLPs, and a solid first choice for an MNIST classifier.
The weakness is dead neurons. If a unit is pushed into the negative side and stays there, it outputs \(0\) and its gradient is \(0\), so the weights that feed it stop receiving updates. A high learning rate, or a bad initialisation, can kill many units this way.








ReLU on top, and its 0-or-1 gradient underneath.











ReLU on top, and its 0-or-1 gradient underneath.





B. GELU
\[
\operatorname{GELU}(x)=x\cdot\Phi(x),
\]
where \(\Phi\) is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal. A widely used approximation is[1]
\[
\operatorname{GELU}(x)\;\approx\;x\cdot\sigma(1.702\,x),
\]
with \(\sigma\) the sigmoid.
GELU is a smooth ReLU. Around zero it has a small negative dip (the minimum is about \(-0.17\)), then it rises almost like a straight line. The gradient is smooth, and neurons rarely die, because a slightly negative input is not hard-zeroed.
It is the standard hidden activation in Transformers such as BERT and GPT[1][3].
SiLU / Swish, \(x\cdot\sigma(x)\), looks almost identical, but its negative dip is deeper: \(\operatorname{SiLU}(-1)\approx-0.269\), against \(\operatorname{GELU}(-1)\approx-0.159\).


C. Sigmoid
\[
\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}.
\]
The range is \((0,1)\), and \(\sigma(0)=0.5\). The derivative is \(\sigma(x)\bigl(1-\sigma(x)\bigr)\), whose maximum is \(0.25\) at \(x=0\). Away from zero the curve flattens, the slope goes toward \(0\), and gradients vanish.
That is why sigmoid is a poor default in hidden layers of a deep net, but it is still the right tool when you need a number in \((0,1)\): a binary output, or a gate in an LSTM.


D. Tanh
\[
\tanh(x)=\frac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{e^{x}+e^{-x}}.
\]
The range is \((-1,1)\), and the output is zero-centred, which is often a kinder hidden representation than a sigmoid that only sits in \((0,1)\). The derivative is \(1-\tanh^{2}(x)\), whose maximum is \(1\) at the origin — four times the peak sigmoid slope — but tanh still saturates in the tails, so gradients can vanish there too.
It is a classic choice in RNNs and LSTMs, and whenever you want a bounded, signed output. It is not a new shape: it is a rescaled sigmoid,
\[
\tanh(x)=2\sigma(2x)-1.
\]


Why language models moved from ReLU to GELU
Compare a single negative input:
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}(-1)=0,\qquad\operatorname{GELU}(-1)\approx-0.159.
\]
ReLU applies a hard cutoff. GELU lets a little of that negative signal through, and the transition is smooth, so the gradient does not jump from \(1\) to \(0\).
GELU was introduced by Hendrycks and Gimpel in 2016[1] and then adopted in BERT and in the GPT family[3]. The catch is important: GELU is not universally better. Its popularity comes from empirical results, not from a theorem that it must win on every task. On a small CNN, ReLU is still often the simpler and faster default.
Later work went a step further. Shazeer (2020) showed that gated linear units, including SwiGLU (a gated SiLU), can improve Transformers[2]. Many later language models use that gated family rather than a plain GELU.


Quiz: Guess the activation function
Four unlabelled curves. Name each one before you open the answers.








Four unlabelled plots, A to D. Guess which activation is which.











Four unlabelled plots, A to D. Guess which activation is which.









Answers






A — ReLU. A hard corner at zero, then a straight line for \(x>0\).
B — GELU. Smooth, almost like ReLU, with a small negative dip.
C — Sigmoid. An S-curve in \((0,1)\), with \(\sigma(0)=0.5\).
D — Tanh. An S-curve in \((-1,1)\), zero-centred.






Python lab
A short numpy and matplotlib walk-through: plot the four functions and their derivatives. Run the cell in a notebook; this page does not execute it at build time.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from math import erf, exp, sqrt, pi

x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 800)

def relu(x):
    return np.maximum(0, x)

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

def tanh(x):
    return np.tanh(x)

def gelu(x):
    # exact GELU: x * Phi(x), with Phi the standard normal CDF
    Phi = np.vectorize(lambda z: 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2))))
    return x * Phi(x)

def relu_grad(x):
    return (x > 0).astype(float)

def sigmoid_grad(x):
    s = sigmoid(x)
    return s * (1 - s)

def tanh_grad(x):
    t = np.tanh(x)
    return 1 - t**2

def gelu_grad(x):
    Phi = np.vectorize(lambda z: 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2))))
    phi = np.exp(-0.5 * x**2) / sqrt(2 * pi)
    return Phi(x) + x * phi

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

axes[0].plot(x, relu(x), label="ReLU")
axes[0].plot(x, gelu(x), label="GELU")
axes[0].plot(x, sigmoid(x), label="Sigmoid")
axes[0].plot(x, tanh(x), label="Tanh")
axes[0].set_title("The four functions")
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.6)

axes[1].plot(x, relu_grad(x), label="ReLU'")
axes[1].plot(x, gelu_grad(x), label="GELU'")
axes[1].plot(x, sigmoid_grad(x), label="Sigmoid'")
axes[1].plot(x, tanh_grad(x), label="Tanh'")
axes[1].set_title("Their derivatives")
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.6)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Rule of thumb

Hidden layers in a CNN or MLP (for example an MNIST classifier): start with ReLU.
Transformers (BERT, GPT and their relatives): GELU, or a later gated variant such as SwiGLU.
Binary outputs and LSTM gates: sigmoid.
Zero-centred, bounded hidden states (classic RNNs): tanh.

If many ReLU units die, lower the learning rate, or try a smooth alternative such as GELU.

FAQ
Why not use a linear activation in every layer? A stack of linear layers is still one linear layer. You need a non-linearity so that depth can learn curved decision surfaces.
What is a dead ReLU? A neuron that always outputs \(0\). Its gradient is \(0\), so the usual update cannot revive it.
Is GELU always better than ReLU? No. GELU won a lot of language-model bake-offs, but that is an empirical pattern, not a proof. On a small vision model, ReLU is still a good default.
If sigmoid shrinks gradients, why is it still taught? Because it is the natural map into \((0,1)\). Use it at an output, or as a gate, not as the hidden activation of a deep stack.
Is softmax an activation of the same kind? Softmax is a vector normalisation used on a multi-class output. It is not a drop-in hidden activation like the four on this page.
Where does the \(1.702\) in the GELU approximation come from? It is the constant Hendrycks and Gimpel fitted so that \(x\cdot\sigma(1.702x)\) tracks \(x\cdot\Phi(x)\) closely[1].

title: ANN: Mathematical Model
text:
Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias term, and applies an activation function. The output of a neuron can be represented as:
\[
y = f\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b \right)
\]
where ( w_i ) are the weights, ( x_i ) are the inputs, ( b ) is the bias, and ( f ) is the activation function.



From: Optical neural networks: progress and challenges


Neuron structure and artificial neural network. a Structure of biological neurons. b Mathematical inferring process of artificial neurons in multi-layer perceptron, including the input, weights, summation, activation function, and output. c Multi-layer perceptron artificial neural network









Simplified model



A biological neuron consists of three main components: dendrites, soma, and axon[2]. Dendrites receive input signals from other neurons. The soma, or cell body, contains the nucleus and processes information. The axon transmits signals to other neurons through synapses[2][8].

An artificial neuron in a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mimics the biological neuron’s function:

Inputs: Represented as a vector [1] \[x = [x_1, x_2, ..., x_n]\]
Weights: Each input is associated with a weight [1] \[w_i\]
Summation: The neuron computes a weighted sum of inputs:
\[v = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i + b\]
where \[b\] is the bias term[1].
Activation Function: The sum is passed through an activation function \[f\]
\[y = f(v)\]
Common activation functions include sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent, and ReLU[1][10].

For the four functions in more detail, including GELU, see Activation functions.

Output: The result \[y\] is the neuron’s output[1].

Multi-layer Perceptron Neural Network
An MLP consists of multiple layers of interconnected neurons:

Input Layer: Receives the initial data[3].
Hidden Layers: Process information through weighted connections and activation functions[3].
Output Layer: Produces the final result[3].

The network learns by adjusting weights and biases through backpropagation, minimizing a cost function[4][9]. This process allows the MLP to model complex relationships between inputs and outputs, making it suitable for various machine learning tasks[3][9].

title: Algorithms: K-Means
text:
Overview
K-Means algorithms classify data into clusters—where K equals the number of clusters. The data points inside of each cluster are homogeneous, and they’re heterogeneous to data points in other clusters.







Clustering is the job of grouping similar points together when nobody has given you the labels in advance.
Think of a market and a mixed pile of fruit. You want \(k\) stalls. You place the stalls, each fruit goes to the nearest stall, then you slide each stall to the middle of its fruit, and you repeat until the stalls barely move. Apples end up with apples and oranges with oranges — even though you never wrote “apple” on a sign.
That procedure is Lloyd’s algorithm, the classic solver for k-means[1].


Lloyd’s loop

Choose \(k\) — how many groups you want. The algorithm does not pick this for you.
Initialise the centres — pick \(k\) starting points in the data. A common choice is k-means++, which spreads the first centres out instead of dropping them all in one corner[2].
Assign — send every point to its nearest centre.
Update — move each centre to the mean (the average position) of the points assigned to it.
Repeat until the assignment stops changing, or you hit a maximum number of passes.






flowchart TD
  A[Choose k] --> B[Place centres]
  B --> C[Assign nearest centre]
  C --> D[Move to the mean]
  D --> E{Still moving?}
  E -->|yes| C
  E -->|no| F[Done]








The objective: inertia, or WCSS
k-means looks for \(k\) centroids that make the clusters as tight as possible. The usual score is the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), also called inertia: the sum of the squared distances from each point to its nearest centre[3]:
\[
J = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2,
\quad a(i)=\arg\min_j\|x_i-c_j\|^2.
\]
The mean squared error (MSE) is the same quantity divided by \(n\). scikit-learn stores inertia as inertia_ after fit. Lower is tighter, but \(J\) always falls as \(k\) grows, so a smaller inertia alone does not mean a better \(k\). Each term \(\lVert x_i-c_{a(i)}\rVert^2\) is a squared L2 norm: how far that point sits from its centre. See ML math symbols and Linear algebra essentials.


k-means++ initialisation
A bad starting set of centres can trap Lloyd in a weak local minimum. k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007) spreads the first centres out: the first centre is chosen at random, and each next one is sampled with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest centre already chosen[2].
It does not remove local minima, and the seeding itself can be slow on very large data, but it is the usual default in scikit-learn and a clear improvement on a purely random start.


Choosing \(k\)
You still have to choose \(k\). Two simple checks:

Elbow. Plot inertia against \(k\). The curve falls quickly at first, then flattens. The “elbow” is a pragmatic guess for \(k\), not a proof.
Silhouette. For each point, compare how close it is to its own cluster versus the next-nearest cluster. The score sits between \(-1\) and \(1\); values near \(1\) mean tight, well-separated groups. Compute the mean silhouette for several \(k\) and prefer a peak.

Neither method is automatic magic. Use them together with what you know about the data.


Limits you should know

You must choose \(k\).
Results are sensitive to initialisation and can stop in a local minimum.
k-means favours compact, roughly spherical clusters of similar size, because each centre is a mean and the distance is Euclidean. Elongated, nested, or very uneven groups can be split badly.
Scale the features. A variable with a huge range will dominate the distances.
Outliers pull the mean, and therefore the centre.
Many iterations may be needed, and each one rereads the whole dataset. One pass compares each of the \(n\) points to all \(k\) centres in \(d\) dimensions, so the work per pass grows with \(n \times k \times d\). Libraries usually cap the number of passes.



Variants

Mini-batch k-means updates the centres from small batches instead of the full dataset. It can be faster on large data, but you have to choose a batch size, and the final error is often a little higher than full-batch Lloyd.
k-medoids uses an actual data point (a medoid) as the centre of each cluster, rather than the mean. That is often more robust to outliers, and it can use other distances than Euclidean.
e-means (2026) keeps the same MSE objective as k-means, but updates centres with mini-batch exponential moving averages and scaling laws that set the batch size and step for you. See e-means.



Python lab
A short scikit-learn walk-through: make a blob dataset, fit k-means, plot the groups, then draw an elbow curve[3].
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X, y_true = make_blobs(
    n_samples=500, centers=4, cluster_std=0.70, random_state=42
)

model = KMeans(n_clusters=4, init="k-means++", n_init=10, random_state=42)
labels = model.fit_predict(X)

plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=labels, s=20)
plt.scatter(
    model.cluster_centers_[:, 0],
    model.cluster_centers_[:, 1],
    c="black",
    s=80,
    marker="x",
)
plt.title("k-means on four blobs")
plt.show()

# Elbow: inertia versus k
ks = range(1, 9)
inertias = []
for k in ks:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init="k-means++", n_init=10, random_state=42)
    km.fit(X)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)

plt.plot(ks, inertias, marker="o")
plt.xlabel("k")
plt.ylabel("inertia (WCSS)")
plt.title("Elbow plot")
plt.show()


Summary



Topic
In brief




Goal
Split unlabelled points into \(k\) tight groups


Loop
Place centres, assign, move each centre to the mean, repeat


Score
Inertia / WCSS (sum of squared distances); MSE is the same quantity divided by \(n\)


Initialisation
k-means++ is the usual default; still a local-minimum method


Choosing \(k\)
Elbow plot of inertia, plus silhouette, plus domain knowledge


Watch out
Scaling, outliers, non-spherical clusters, many full-dataset passes


A faster variant
e-means, when you already use a high-performance k-means





FAQ
Is \(k\) learned from the data? No. You choose \(k\), then the algorithm places the centres.
Does k-means++ always find the global best clustering? No. It is a better start, not a guarantee. Several restarts (n_init in scikit-learn) are still useful.
Why did my features need scaling? Distances are Euclidean. A feature measured in thousands will drown one measured in units, unless you scale them.
When should I try e-means instead? When the dataset is large and many Lloyd passes are the bottleneck. For a small scikit-learn problem, classic k-means is usually enough. See e-means.


See also
For a faster drop-in replacement of Lloyd’s k-means, with mini-batch exponential moving averages and no extra hyperparameter sweep, see e-means.
The inertia terms are squared L2 norms; a short reminder is in ML math symbols and Linear algebra essentials.


References

[1] Stuart P. Lloyd, Least squares quantization in PCM, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 28(2):129–137, 1982. https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1982.1056489
[2] David Arthur and Sergei Vassilvitskii, k-means++: The advantages of careful seeding, Proceedings of SODA, 2007, pp. 1027–1035. ACM DL, author PDF
[3] scikit-learn documentation, Clustering: K-means. https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#k-means, and sklearn.cluster.KMeans

title: Algorithms: Introduction
text:
Machine learning algorithms are sets of instructions that enable computers to learn from data, identify patterns, and make predictions without explicit programming.


What you can do with machine learning algorithms
Machine learning algorithms help you answer questions that are too complex to answer through manual analysis.
Use cases for machine learning algorithms typically fall into one of these categories:

Predict a target,
Find unusual data points,
Predict values,
See how values change over time,
Discover similarities,
Classification

These algorithms form the backbone of machine learning systems, allowing machines to improve their performance over time as they process more data.
At their core, machine learning algorithms:

Analyze large amounts of data
Discover patterns and relationships
Make decisions or predictions based on the learned patterns

Machine learning algorithms are typically categorized into three main types:

Supervised Learning: algorithms make predictions based on a set of labeled examples that you provide.

This technique is useful when you know what the outcome should look like.

Unsupervised Learning: the data points aren’t labeled—the algorithm labels them for you by organizing the data or describing its structure.

This technique is useful when you don’t know what the outcome should look like.

Reinforcement Learning: uses algorithms that learn from outcomes and decide which action to take next.

After each action, the algorithm receives feedback that helps it determine whether the choice it made was correct, neutral, or incorrect.
It’s a good technique to use for automated systems that have to make a lot of small decisions without human guidance.
For example, you’re designing an autonomous car, and you want to ensure that it’s obeying the law and keeping people safe. As the car gains experience and a history of reinforcement, it learns how to stay in its lane, go the speed limit, and brake for pedestrians.








Machine learning algorithms



Machine learning algorithms are mathematical models that implement a finite set of unambiguous step-by-step instructions to achieve a specific goal, such as classification, regression, or clustering. They utilize statistical techniques to enable computers to “learn” from data without being explicitly programmed[1].

title: Algorithms: e-means
text:
New (Nov 2026)



The paper is fresh and not yet peer reviewed; speedups are as reported by the authors.



Classic k-means, in brief
k-means groups unlabelled points into \(k\) clusters. Lloyd’s algorithm places \(k\) centres, assigns each point to the nearest one, moves each centre to the mean of its points, and repeats. That is the same goal e-means keeps. For the full walk-through — the loop, inertia, k-means++, how to choose \(k\), and a scikit-learn lab — see k-means.
e-means keeps the same \(k\) centroids and the same MSE, but needs far fewer passes over the data. The rest of this page explains what changes, and what the authors report.


Overview
e-means is a drop-in replacement for Lloyd’s k-means. It solves the same clustering problem — minimise the mean squared distance of each point to its nearest centroid — but updates those centroids with mini-batch exponential moving averages, so it usually reaches a lower loss in far fewer passes over the data.
It was introduced in November 2026 by Swann Bessa and colleagues at FAIR at Meta and École Nationale des Ponts et Chaussées, and shipped in Faiss 1.16.0[1][2][3].






Same problem, different optimiser



e-means is not a new kind of clustering. The inputs are still the dataset and the number of clusters k. The outputs are still \(k\) centroids and an assignment. What changes is how the centroids move: mini-batches, an exponential moving average, and scaling laws that set the batch size and step size for you[1][3].


The announcement thread, the paper, and the project site (with a browser playground) are the primary sources for this page.


What e-means changes
Think of Lloyd as a teacher who only moves the classroom desks after taking attendance of every student. One complete roll-call, then one simultaneous move.
e-means walks the room in small groups. After each group, every desk slides a little toward the students currently sitting there. The slide is an exponential moving average (EMA): the desk does not jump to the latest group, and it does not forget the groups that came before. It blends the new evidence with what it already knew — like a thermostat that does not slam to the latest reading.
Earlier mini-batch k-means methods (MacQueen, Sculley) already update from small batches instead of the full dataset. They can be faster, but when they have been compared with Lloyd they typically finish at a higher error, and the practitioner has to guess a batch size and a step size[1].







Still from a 2D comparison of Lloyd (full batch) and e-means on the same point clouds.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. A still from the animation in post 3/10: side-by-side Lloyd and e-means, with training MSE against the number of passes.
The authors specialise the EMA rule for a fixed dataset (the usual k-means setting), rather than for a shifting codebook as in VQ-VAEs[1]:

Automatic batch size and step size. Scaling laws, fitted on the DEEP dataset and checked on held-out sets, choose the batch size \(B\) and the initial step \(\alpha_0\) from \(n\), \(k\), and the epoch budget \(T\). You do not run a hyperparameter sweep[1][2].








Diagram of the scaling laws that set batch size and step from n, k and the epoch budget.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. Post 5/10: \(n\), \(k\) and \(T\) go in; batch size \(B\) and step \(\alpha_0\) come out.

A decaying step. The step \(\alpha=1-\gamma\) follows a cosine schedule, from \(\alpha_0\) down to \(0.1\,\alpha_0\), so the centroids settle as training goes on[1].
Dead-cluster revival. If a cluster stops receiving points, e-means periodically splits a busy “donor” cluster into two, following the same idea Faiss uses for Lloyd. The authors report this as the most important ingredient in their ablation[1][2].








Side-by-side 2D clustering with revival off and revival on.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. A still from the bonus animation in post 10/10, comparing dead-cluster revival off and on.

A cheap finalisation. After the last epoch, each centroid is replaced by the exact mean of the points assigned to it in that last pass (the default, which helps training MSE). A slower EMA of the centroids is offered when the goal is out-of-sample (test) MSE[1].

By default e-means starts from a random sample of the data, not from k-means++. The paper finds that k-means++ can shave a little more loss, but its cost is high; for a small epoch budget it is usually better to train a bit longer instead[1].





flowchart TD
  A[Take a mini-batch] --> B[Assign nearest centre]
  B --> C[EMA-update counts and sums]
  C --> D[Revive dead clusters]
  D --> A
  C --> E[Last epoch: exact mean]








Results, as reported by the authors
These figures come from the paper and the announcement thread. They are the authors’ own measurements, mostly on embedding datasets, against strong library baselines — not a re-run on this wiki[1][2].



Claim
What the authors report
Source




Epochs to beat Lloyd at 25 iterations
On a wide array of embedding datasets, e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs
Paper abstract[1]


GPU wall-clock
That epoch advantage is reported as 10–45× in the abstract, and as 9.5× to 45.5× versus Flash-KMeans in Table 4 (medians over seeds, up to 1 billion points)
Abstract and Table 4[1]


Quality at a short budget
Three epochs of e-means from random initialisation beat Flash-KMeans at 25 iterations on all eight main setups in Table 5; after five epochs it also stays ahead of Flash-KMeans with greedy k-means++ initialisation
Table 5[1]


Very large scale
On DINO10B (10 billion DINO embeddings), e-means partitions the data into 16 million clusters in 2.5 epochs, with a loss below Lloyd at 25 epochs
Abstract[1]


Coverage
The thread describes evaluation on 26 datasets, from 100k to 10 billion points, with a results map
Thread, post 6/10[2]



The 10× headline is a comparison with state-of-the-art implementations (Faiss on CPU, Flash-KMeans on GPU), not with a naïve Python loop. Swann Bessa made that distinction in the thread[2].







Histograms of train and test MSE: e-means from a random start versus Lloyd with random and k-means++ initialisation.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. Post 4/10: on these embedding datasets, e-means from a random initialisation (blue) often finishes at a lower loss than Lloyd, including Lloyd with greedy k-means++ (green).







Test loss against epochs, and wall-clock time on CPU and GPU.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. Post 7/10, on DEEP with 1 million vectors and 16,384 clusters. The annotated speedups (12.5× fewer epochs, 11.8× CPU, 13.6× GPU) are the authors’ labels on this figure.







Aggregated GPU time against dataset size, with and without IVF assignment.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. Post 8/10: at billion scale the authors pair e-means with an IVF index for a further wall-clock cut.






A limitation, also from the paper



The scaling laws were tuned for relatively high-dimensional embedding data. The authors say they are not optimal on very low-dimensional and tiny datasets[1]. In Faiss, the defaults already change in that regime: for \(d \le 16\) the “quality” (smaller) batch law is used, and for \(d \le 2\) dead-cluster revival is turned off[3].




How to try it in Faiss
e-means ships in Faiss 1.16.0 as faiss.contrib.e_means. On CPU, faiss-cpu is enough. On GPU, training runs through PyTorch (with optional Triton or CuTe kernels); the data must already be on the GPU[2][3].
The snippet below follows the official Faiss user guide. Default nepochs is 5, which the authors describe as typically enough to beat Lloyd’s loss at convergence[3].
import numpy as np
from faiss.contrib.e_means import NumpyEmeans

x = np.random.rand(200_000, 64).astype("float32")

em = NumpyEmeans(64, 500)          # d=64, k=500; 5 epochs by default
centroids, labels = em.train(x)    # centroids: (500, 64)

x_new = np.random.rand(100_000, 64).astype("float32")
distances, new_labels = em.assign(x_new)
On a GPU, import Emeans and pass a tensor that is already on the device:
import torch
from faiss.contrib.e_means import Emeans

xg = torch.from_numpy(x).cuda().to(torch.bfloat16)
em = Emeans(64, 1024)
centroids, labels = em.train(xg)
labels from train are the assignments from the last training epoch. Because the centroids still moved during that epoch, they are not always each vector’s nearest final centroid. For exact nearest-centroid labels, call assign on the training set as well[3].


When to use it
A good default when you already cluster with Faiss or another high-performance k-means, especially on large embedding sets, IVF codebook training, or any job where 25 Lloyd iterations are the bottleneck[1][2].
Stay with ordinary k-means for tiny or very low-dimensional problems (the laws are not tuned for them), or when you only have scikit-learn and a small dataset where Lloyd is already cheap. e-means is in Faiss, not in scikit-learn. See the k-means lab for that path.
e-means speeds up training of an IVF index. It is not a claim about later search latency once that index is built; the paper discusses the effect on recall in Appendix L[1][2].


Summary









Lloyd k-means
e-means




Objective
Minimise MSE to \(k\) centroids
The same


Update
Full-dataset mean, each epoch
Mini-batch EMA, then a last-epoch mean


Extra knobs beyond \(k\) and epochs
None in the usual Faiss call
None required: batch size and step come from scaling laws


Typical budget in the paper
25 epochs as the Faiss-style reference
1.4–2.6 epochs to pass that reference loss, 5 by default in Faiss


Initialisation in the main experiments
Often k-means++
Random sample of the data


Where it lives
Faiss Kmeans, scikit-learn, and many other libraries
Faiss 1.16.0, faiss.contrib.e_means





FAQ
Is the “e” a new distance or a new cluster shape? No. The “e” is for the exponential moving average used to update the centroids[1][3].
Do I still choose \(k\)? Yes. \(k\) is still the main modelling choice. The batch size and step size are the parts e-means can set for you[1][3].
Why is it faster if each epoch still assigns points to centroids? The assignment work per epoch is comparable to Lloyd. The speed-up comes from needing many fewer epochs (and from specialised kernels that turn that into wall-clock savings)[1].

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are computational models inspired by the biological neural networks found in human brains, designed to process complex data and perform tasks such as classification, prediction, and pattern recognition.







The Basic Layers in ANN


Their architecture typically comprises three layers:

an input layer that receives data,
one or more hidden layers that perform processing through interconnected nodes (neurons),
and an output layer that delivers the final result.

ANNs are widely recognized for their ability to learn from large datasets, making them pivotal in various applications, including image and speech recognition, natural language processing, and medical diagnosis[1][2].


The growing significance of ANNs stems from their versatility and effectiveness across multiple domains, from enhancing customer experiences in eCommerce through personalized recommendations to advancing medical technologies by aiding in disease diagnosis and treatment planning[3][4].
However, their deployment also raises important ethical considerations, particularly regarding bias, accountability, and the implications of automated decision-making in sensitive fields such as healthcare.
As organizations increasingly integrate ANNs into their operations, issues of transparency and interpretability have emerged as critical concerns, challenging the trustworthiness of these models in high-stakes applications[5][6].
Various types of ANNs, including Feedforward Neural Networks (FNNs), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), cater to different tasks and data structures, each offering unique advantages.

For instance, CNNs excel in image-related tasks by identifying spatial hierarchies in data, while RNNs are adept at processing sequential data, such as time series or natural language, by maintaining context across inputs[7][8].

Despite their transformative potential, ANNs face challenges, including the risk of overfitting, the requirement for extensive training data, and the computational resources needed for effective training.
Furthermore, the complex nature of ANNs often leads to their characterization as “black boxes,” making it difficult to interpret the decision-making processes involved.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are structured to mimic the interconnected network of neurons in the human brain, facilitating complex information processing.
The architecture of an ANN typically consists of three main types of layers: the input layer, hidden layers, and the output layer.

Input Layer
The input layer serves as the initial point of data entry for the neural network. It receives information from the external environment in various forms such as numbers, letters, audio files, or image pixels.
Each node in the input layer corresponds to a specific feature of the data being processed, and it plays a critical role in transmitting this information to subsequent layers for further analysis[1][2].
Hidden Layers
Hidden layers are positioned between the input and output layers and are responsible for the majority of the processing within the ANN. A network may have one or multiple hidden layers, each containing numerous artificial neurons.
These layers perform complex mathematical operations on the input data, identifying patterns and relationships that are not immediately apparent. The output from one hidden layer becomes the input for the next layer, allowing for a deeper analysis of the data at each stage[1][3][2].

Types of Hidden Layers: Hidden layers can vary in their configuration and function. They may employ different types of activation functions, which introduce non-linear properties to the network, enabling it to learn complex mappings from inputs to outputs.
The choice of activation function can significantly impact the performance of the neural network in various tasks[4][5].

For a walk-through of ReLU, sigmoid, tanh and GELU, see Activation functions.
Output Layer
The output layer is the final layer in the ANN structure and provides the ultimate result of the computations performed by the network. Depending on the nature of the task, the output layer can contain a single node for binary classification or multiple nodes for multi-class classification problems.
Each output node generates a response based on the processed information, translating the network’s findings into actionable insights or predictions[1][3][5].
